articles.title: A day-one briefing for Apple’s new CEO
articles.text:
Executive Summary, Day One
📁 Inbox 5:05AM
To: Ternus, John <jternus@apple.com>
Reply-to: CEO-transition-team@apple.com
A day-one briefing for Apple’s new CEO
An executive summary to get John Ternus up to speed.
A day-one briefing for Apple’s new CEO
An executive summary to get John Ternus up to speed.
Welcome to your first day as CEO! Hopefully you’re finding your new office spacious and comfortable. If you have trouble with any of the doors just ping us — being a Jony Ive design, you won’t find anything as unsightly as a door handle here!
Today’s memo includes a summary of the business, broken out by division. The day’s schedule is also attached; please note that the Apple Intelligence team needed to delay the new Siri discussion until a later date, but they promise they’re “for real” this time.
Hardware
Everything is in hand for the upcoming phone launches. We don’t anticipate the price hikes will have much impact on sales, since nobody in the US knows how much they really pay for their phone anyway. The team agrees that calling the camera on the upcoming AirPods a “sensor” would make it less creepy and is moving forward with that terminology. Morale on the Vision Pro team after their move to the basement is somewhat low, but we’ve scheduled a virtual offsite for them in Tahiti that we think will help.
Services
Our new EU app store rules go into effect in exactly one month. We’ve compiled a simplified explainer breaking down how much commission app developers will pay and which companies can operate alternative app stores into an easy-to-parse, 300-page PDF (see attached). This does mean that our services revenue will take a hit, but on the bright side, we just rolled out ads in Maps to juice the numbers.
Despite the setbacks, services is still our best bet for growth since we, well, ran out of people to sell iPhones to. It might even become a bigger business than the iPhone someday. That could fundamentally change the kind of company Apple is — a hardware guy in charge of a services company? Or will a services company pivot back to hardware under a new CEO? Striking that balance without frustrating customers remains an ongoing challenge. Take a hint from your predecessor: Ted Lasso is so lovable nobody noticed that we raised Apple TV prices again.
Software
The good news is that the updated Liquid Glass design is polling with higher approval ratings than last year. The bad news is that Brussels is still mad at us for holding back new Siri in Europe, Google’s kind of eating our lunch in the EU, and app developers are still unhappy with the new commission structure. We were, uh, not winning any popularity contests with app developers to start with, so this may be something to consider.
Operation Smarter Siri Take Two has been a success, and we’re finally back in the AI game. Unfortunately, in the time that passed since Smarter Siri The First Try, AI became deeply unfashionable. But it kind of works in our favor; we can let Meta and Google take the heat on building out all those data centers (pun intended?) while we cajole app developers into using app intents so Siri can actually do stuff. Once again, see above point about developers.
Side note: Alan Dye was seen near campus holding a sign that reads “Liquid Glass is good, actually” but security handled it.
Special Projects
The car lab has transitioned nicely into the new AI wearable testing / smart home facility. There’s a little conflict between the sleep tracking team and the Beats team over the noise level in the test house, but we gave the sleepers some AirPods with noise cancellation, which should resolve the issue. Oh, and the Pope has expressed interest in trying the AI Siri pin. He loves his Apple Watch, and apparently His Holiness would like a screen-free way to brush up on his White Sox trivia in his downtime.
At least Meta is giving us a pretty low hurdle to clear, right?
Sentiment among beta testers on the smart glasses is a tad low — “Creepy as F—” tends to come up a lot in feedback. The team remains confident and has some anti-creep modifications planned. At least Meta is giving us a pretty low hurdle to clear, right? This might be a segment to pay attention to after you’re settled in. There are growing concerns in how we can maintain our stance on privacy while putting cameras on people’s ears and in their glasses.
Upcoming Key Activities
Just a reminder of some upcoming events: The team is gathering tomorrow night for drinks celebrating Phil’s not-quite-retirement. Tim’s goodbye drinks thing is tonight, and as a parting gift, he wants to review last quarter’s production numbers, for old time’s sake. He really does have a different idea of “fun,” doesn’t he? He’ll be heading to DC immediately after; President Trump has requested his help troubleshooting an issue with his iPad. Also, you’ll find Kate’s retirement party on your calendar. And Jennifer’s retirement party. That’s a lot of exits, huh? At least Craig still insists he isn’t going anywhere. We’re keeping a close eye on him anyway.
Of course, there’s your big debut as CEO coming up next week. Rehearsals have looked great — you’ve really been studying the Cook-ian “Good Morning!” bellow. Sure, investors will be looking for any sign of weakness. And a big price hike just as we’re introducing a new boss isn’t great timing. There’s a lot hinging on this keynote, you could say.
If there’s any way we can help make your first day better, don’t hesitate. Just relax and remember you’re running the world’s most profitable company in a time of political uncertainty, a historic supply chain crisis, unprecedented governmental scrutiny, and top executive shuffling. No pressure, Big J! You got this. Time to surprise and shine!

articles.title: The Pentagon now has its own version of ChatGPT and Grok | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Pentagon has launched versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok, giving 3 million civilian and military personnel access to generative AI tools that have been tailored to “warfighter needs.”
ChatGPT Mil and Grok for Government — custom versions of the popular consumer generative AI tools — are now part of GenAI.mil, a centralized, secure portal launched last year.
GenAI.mil, which offered Google Gemini when it first launched, is designed to give Department of Defense employees access to commercial frontier AI models without sending sensitive government data through ordinary consumer channels. In particular, the official military version is exempt from the data collection that is difficult to avoid in consumer tech products.
And according to the Department of Defense, the generative AI portal has proven popular. GenAI.mil has already onboarded more than 1.7 million unique users out of the department’s 3 million personnel, according to the department.
These latest additions are part of the Pentagon’s broader effort to use AI tools to accelerate work and give the Department of Defense an edge without sacrificing security. They also highlight the absence of Anthropic’s Claude model and the Pentagon’s effort to work with other companies following its dispute with the frontier lab. Anthropic was labeled a supply-chain risk by the Trump administration — a designation that it is currently fighting in court — after it refused to give the Pentagon unrestricted use of its AI tools and instead insisted on certain safety guardrails.
ChatGPT Mil, which came out of the company’s OpenAI for Government program, will offer an experience familiar to commercial ChatGPT users. The tool will focus on chat, files, projects, and custom GPTs, according to the Defense Department. The tool will also support document-heavy, routine unclassified work such as administrative tasks, logistics, planning, and policy. Other features will be added over time.
The Pentagon positioned Grok’s capabilities and potential uses in much broader and more militaristic terms.
“Starshield AI’s Grok for Government will provide the warfighter with immediate productivity gains, stronger knowledge continuity and more secure and efficient collaboration,” according to the Defense Department’s press release. (SpaceX’s Starshield AI is a secure satellite network that uses the company’s existing Starlink tech.)
The department added that Grok would allow its military “to execute missions faster and with greater precision across numerous operational contexts, ranging from market research analysis for acquisition professionals to supply-chain management for logisticians.”
The Pentagon has struck deals with a number of other tech companies in a bid to boost its AI capabilities, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Reflection AI.

articles.title: How Zambia’s Kulanda House is building an ecosystem of contextual learning materials for African children - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Zambia’s Kulanda House is building an ecosystem of contextual learning materials for African children, with a host of platforms that help kids learn in different ways.
Founded in 2022 by CEO Kapampa Mwape and creative director David Gondwe, Kulanda House initially launched operations with Suku Books, which turns Zambian folktales and proverbs into engaging, curriculum-aligned storybooks and levelled readers.
“These are books children actually connect to because the world in them is the one they see every day. Suku Books are our foundation and our way into schools,” Mwape told Disrupt Africa.
“On top of that content we have the Kula Kids web platform where teachers plan, assign reading, track each child’s literacy development, and see who’s progressing and who’s stuck, with parents kept informed through their own dashboard.”
Children read interactively and learn through educational games, while teachers get the data they need to effectively teach. Mwape said the startup’s mission is to strengthen early literacy through accessible, high-quality materials that honour African identity and support teachers and families.
The idea began when Mwape and Gondwe were paired on a project while studying together. Each co-founder had grown up with opposite experiences.
“I loved and read books often whereas my co-founder didn’t enjoy it because he hadn’t been given the support where he struggled, but he had experienced the beauty of African storytelling and loved it. That contrast is what grounded Kulanda’s mission,” said Mwape.
Kulanda House fills in a gap from three different angles – international publishers have great distribution but foreign content that lacks deep meaning for the African child, local materials have the contextual fit but often lack structure and distribution, while classroom management remains a problem for teachers teaching over 50 children daily with limited insight and tracking.
“Our hybrid of physical books and a digital platform closes these gaps,” said Mwape.
Bootstrapped thus far, the company has sold over 6,000 books to individuals and institutions. Kula Kids is currently in the school-testing phase to see whether schools will sustain recurring membership with the data provided from the platform.
“We would like to prove the model in this market before we expand it further, but our initial aim is to expand into Southern and East Africa,” said Mwape.

articles.title: Creating Short Fiction Scenes from Simple Prompts - Tech Guide
articles.text:
A writer thinks they have a simple idea: “A person realizes they’ve made a terrible mistake.” That’s it. Four words that contain infinite possibility. 
Every human has experienced that moment of sudden clarity where past actions reveal themselves as catastrophic. The simplicity of the prompt masks its richness.
Text to video generation transforms these simple fiction prompts into generated footage that captures that singular moment with all its emotional weight intact, allowing a basic story concept to become a complete scene where tension, character, and consequence unfold visually.
Dreamina’s Seedance 2.5 model was engineered to understand how to extract emotional and narrative complexity from deceptively simple prompts, rendering short fiction moments that carry the full weight of human experience despite their apparent simplicity.
The genius of constraint
Short fiction thrives on limitation. A novelist has three hundred pages to develop character and explore theme. A short fiction writer has perhaps three thousand words, sometimes far fewer. That constraint forces ruthless prioritization — every sentence must earn its place, every scene must advance understanding, every moment must matter. This isn’t a handicap; it’s an advantage. Constraint breeds creativity by forcing clarity about what actually matters.
Why simple prompts generate powerful fiction
A paradox exists at the heart of storytelling: the simpler the premise, the more room for meaningful interpretation. A complex, detailed prompt leaves little for a viewer to project onto a scene. A simple prompt invites viewers to recognize themselves in the story, to project their own experiences onto the situation, to complete the emotional picture themselves. That collaborative relationship between creator and viewer is what makes simple fiction prompts so powerful.
Text-to-video actually strengthens this dynamic. A generated scene from a simple prompt doesn’t have a specific actor’s face or particular physical details that might not match a viewer’s imagination.
Character revealed through crisis
Short fiction often skips character introduction entirely and instead reveals character through how someone responds to pressure. A person facing consequences reveals what they actually value through their choices. A character in conflict reveals their priorities through what they’re willing to sacrifice. This approach to characterization is perfect for generated fiction because the generator doesn’t need to show years of development — it only needs to render a moment where character becomes undeniably visible.
A simple prompt about crisis is often more effective than an elaborate character biography. “A person confronting someone they’ve wronged” reveals character through that confrontation more effectively than pages of backstory.
The Power of Seedance 2.5 for Short Fiction
Seedance 2.5 was designed to render brief narrative moments with the emotional precision and character authenticity that make short fiction deeply affecting despite its brevity.
Authentic facial expression and micro-emotion
The model captures subtle shifts in expression that communicate internal state without requiring dialogue or explanation. A character’s realization, doubt, regret, or determination becomes readable through small changes that feel genuine rather than performed.
Natural dialogue delivery with emotional subtext
Dialogue carries layers of meaning beyond literal words. Seedance 2.5 renders how a character says something as much as what they say, making subtext visible and emotional truth apparent through vocal performance.
Spatial storytelling through composition
Character positioning and movement communicate relationship dynamics and emotional stakes. The model understands compositional choices that reveal conflict, connection, or tension through how characters occupy space relative to each other.
Emotional pacing that respects story rhythm
Extended duration allows emotional beats to land with appropriate weight. A revelation needs silence around it. A confrontation needs time to develop. Seedance 2.5 renders pacing that matches the story’s emotional rhythm rather than rushing through narrative.
From prompt to powerful scene
Step 1: Clarify your story’s central moment and create your prompt
Visit Dreamina, sign in, and head to the “AI Video” section. Identify the single moment where your story’s emotional truth becomes most visible. Is it a realization? A confrontation? A decision? A discovery? Click “Add reference image” if you have visual references or mood boards that capture the scene’s tone. Write your fiction prompt focusing on that central moment, describing the character’s internal state, the conflict or stakes, and how the setting participates in the story.
A detailed prompt for a 30-second scene might read: A person sits alone in their car after losing their job, hands gripping the steering wheel, processing the immediate future suddenly becoming uncertain, the familiar parking lot now feeling hostile, their expression cycling through denial to acceptance, the moment where life pivots, shot through the windshield with city lights creating ambient atmosphere, mood devastated but oddly clear. 
Step 2: Generate your fiction scene with Seedance 2.5
Select the Seedance 2.5 model for generation. Choose 30-45 seconds for focused story moments — enough time for emotional beats to land without excess. Pick 16:9 for short film contexts or 9:16 for social platforms. Click Dreamina’s generation icon and watch your simple prompt transform into a complete, emotionally resonant scene.
Step 3: Refine emotional impact and finalize your fiction
Use Dreamina’s AI editing tools to enhance what matters. Upscale sharpens facial expressions and details that communicate emotion, while Generate Soundtrack adds ambient audio that reinforces emotional atmosphere. Review your generated scene — do the emotional beats land? Is the character’s internal state readable? Does the setting participate meaningfully in the story? Once your simple prompt has been rendered into a scene with genuine emotional power, export and share your short fiction creation.
Dialogue as story engine
Short fiction often relies heavily on dialogue because conversation is efficient storytelling. Two characters talking reveal relationship, conflict, stakes, and theme simultaneously. A single exchange can communicate more than paragraphs of narration. This dialogue-driven approach works beautifully with text to video because generated scenes can render how dialogue sounds and lands emotionally rather than just how it reads on a page.
A simple prompt about two characters having one conversation can become a complete scene where their relationship, conflict, and emotional stakes all become visible through dialogue delivery, physical response, and spatial relationship. The simplicity of “two people talking” contains narrative richness that generated footage can make fully visible.
When simplicity contains everything
The most affecting short fiction often emerges from the simplest prompts because simplicity forces clarity about what actually matters. With Dreamina and its Seedance 2.5 model, a basic story idea can become generated footage that captures the full emotional and narrative weight of human experience.
It allows text-to-video to transform simple fiction prompts into powerful scenes that stay with viewers long after they finish watching.

articles.title: Comment renommer son smartphone (iPhone et Android) et pourquoi c’est utile
articles.text:
À la sortie de la boîte, un smartphone affiche souvent un nom générique (« iPhone », « Pixel », « Galaxy »). Ce libellé, visible lors d’un appairage Bluetooth ou d’un partage de connexion, n’a rien à voir avec l’identifiant unique de l’appareil ou son numéro de série : c’est une étiquette modifiable, utile pour repérer rapidement son mobile parmi d’autres.
Mais pourquoi changer ce nom ?
Renommer son appareil permet de l’identifier facilement quand on le connecte à une voiture, un ordinateur, des écouteurs ou un réseau partagé. Cela évite les confusions dans un foyer avec plusieurs téléphones similaires ou bien lors d’évènements type concert où beaucoup de personnes utiliseraient un appareil portant le même nom.
Nous allons donc vous montrer rapidement comment modifier ce nom. Petit conseil avant de se plonger dans ce tutoriel : évitez d’inclure des informations personnelles (nom de famille, numéro, email) dans le nom de l’appareil : ce libellé est visible publiquement dès qu’un Bluetooth, un Quick Share ou un hotspot est détecté à proximité.
iOS : un seul réglage pour tout
Sur iPhone, la personnalisation est centralisée :
Allez dans Réglages > Général > Informations > Nom.
Le nouveau nom s’applique immédiatement à iCloud, AirDrop, Bluetooth, l’ordinateur associé et au point d’accès personnel (le SSID du hotspot suit ce changement, sans toucher au mot de passe).
Android : des menus variables selon la marque
Sur Android, l’emplacement du réglage dépend du constructeur. Voici quelques exemples :
- Samsung : Paramètres > À propos du téléphone, puis appuyez sur Modifier à côté du nom.
- Xiaomi / Motorola : le menu peut varier. Le mieux étant d’effectuer une recherche avec les termes « nom de l’appareil » dans les paramètres pour y accéder vite.
- Google Pixel : Paramètres > Appareils connectés > Préférences de connexion > Bluetooth > Nom de l’appareil (le Bluetooth doit être activé pour que le changement soit visible).
Quick Share et la visibilité
Le partage de fichiers à proximité d’Android, Quick Share, utilise aussi ce nom, mais ajoute un contrôle de visibilité : Dans Paramètres Quick Share, la section « Qui peut partager du contenu avec vous » permet de limiter aux appareils personnels, aux contacts, ou à tout le monde pendant 10 minutes.
Cette option temporaire évite de rester visible en permanence, un principe proche d’AirDrop côté Apple.
Point d’accès WiFi : un nom indépendant sur Android
Pour terminer, petite astuce : sachez que, contrairement à l’iPhone, de nombreux smartphones Android permettent de définir un SSID différent pour le point d’accès WiFi. Très concrètement, vous pouvez ainsi plus facilement partager votre WiFi sans dévoiler le nom de votre appareil.
Pour ce faire, voici la marche à suivre : Paramètres > Réseaux et Internet (ou Connexions) > Point d’accès WiFi.
Notre recommandation est donc la suivante : opter pour un nom discret pour le partage de données et un nom plus explicite pour l’appairage Bluetooth et Quick Share.

 Points forts
- Écran ultra lumineux.
- Performances de haute volée.
- Excellente autonomie.
- Polyvalence photo et vidéo.
Points faibles
- Charge que l'on aimerait plus rapide.
- S Pen sans Bluetooth.
Le Galaxy S24 Ultra avait rempli tous les critères attendus d'un smartphone très haut de gamme, et Samsung fait aussi bien, sinon mieux, avec son Galaxy S25 Ultra. Le terminal est une réussite incontestable sur le plan technique et se paie le luxe de gagner en puissance comme en endurance, tout en conservant son talon d'Achille (minime, il faut bien le dire), à savoir sa charge pas vraiment rapide. Son seul véritable problème n'en est un que pour les plus férus de téléphonie : si l'on excepte son volet logiciel dopé à l'IA, il n'apporte pas de véritable nouveauté à son prédécesseur. Il se frotte dès lors à la même difficulté que ses concurrents ; alors que la téléphonie a atteint un plateau technique, comment se démarquer, si ce n'est par des fonctionnalités logicielles ? Pour résumer, il manque peut-être au Galaxy S25 Ultra ce que l'on pourrait qualifier de petit supplément d'âme pour non seulement convaincre (ce qu'il fait sans peine), mais aussi séduire. Mais tout cela n'est que chipotage, puisqu'à notre sens, c'est l'efficacité qui prime.

articles.title: SUSE Positions Hardware Choice as a Core Part of Sovereign AI - EE Times
articles.text:
SUSE is positioning architectural choice as a key element of sovereign AI. It argues that enterprises should be able to use Nvidia accelerators today without having to rebuild their AI infrastructure if they later switch to another silicon platform.
This hardware portability reflects a broader shift in how SUSE defines sovereignty—not as eliminating external dependencies, but as giving enterprises the flexibility to change or replace those dependencies.
“The honest answer is every organization needs to decide its own risk profile on this spectrum,” Rhys Oxenham, VP and general manager, AI, at SUSE, said. “Full sovereignty at every layer isn’t realistic today, but architectural choice at each layer is.”
SUSE launched AI Factory with Nvidia in April as an infrastructure stack for enterprises building and running AI workloads across data center, edge, and cloud environments. For customers using SUSE AI Factory with Nvidia, the platform runs on SUSE Linux Enterprise Server and SUSE Kubernetes Engine, with Nvidia AI Enterprise embedded inside SUSE’s governance and security layer.
According to SUSE, this allows enterprises to keep their AI workloads within customer-controlled infrastructure rather than relying on third-party APIs.
“Customers choose a dependency on Nvidia at the accelerated compute layer itself, specifically CUDA, the GPU operator, and the NIM microservices that ship as part of Nvidia AI Enterprise,” Oxenham said. “That is a deliberate, pragmatic tradeoff for top-tier speed and performance, with a pre-validated, fast-to-deploy stack rather than something hand-built from scratch.”
An enterprise using SUSE AI Factory with Nvidia is therefore still dependent on Nvidia at the accelerated-compute layer. SUSE’s argument is that this dependency does not necessarily extend through the rest of the infrastructure stack.
The company said the underlying AI Factory architecture remains hardware agnostic, allowing organizations to move to other accelerator ecosystems without replatforming.
The company is also working with organizations running accelerator platforms other than Nvidia. At AMD Advancing AI 2026, SUSE announced support for AMD silicon and its GPU operator within SUSE AI Factory. According to AMD’s technical blog, SUSE has validated the AMD Instinct MI350P accelerator alongside its software blueprint engineering work.
Linux and Kubernetes provide the abstraction layers above the hardware.
“Organizations don’t need to replatform, redesign cluster topologies, or rewrite operational playbooks just because they are introducing a new accelerator,” Oxenham said.
The changes are primarily limited to silicon-native dependencies at the bottom of the stack, at the Linux layer. These include drivers and GPU operators, along with corresponding runtime libraries such as AMD’s ROCm and Nvidia’s CUDA runtime environments.
SUSE said the broader AI software ecosystem can support both implementations, which can reduce the changes required when customers move between accelerators. The approach is intended to allow workloads to run across different accelerator platforms as supply, cost, and performance requirements change.
Managing vs. eliminating dependency
SUSE applies the same principle beyond silicon to AI models and APIs. Enterprises can use proprietary AI models and services, but SUSE argues that they should avoid dependencies that make it difficult to switch later.
“If, as an organization, you are building against proprietary, you are becoming much more locked into that implementation and you subject yourself to two core problems,” Oxenham said.
The first is cost. If API prices increase, organizations remain tied to those services, and costs rise with usage.
The second is access. “As we saw in a number of different events over the last few months, certain models were restricted for certain jurisdictions,” Oxenham said. “If you had built your intelligence based around a particular implementation, then you would have been immediately shut off from that implementation.”
Oxenham also pointed to the growing capability of open-weight models as another way to reduce dependence on proprietary AI services. “The capabilities of some of the latest open-weight models, when benchmarked against the latest frontier models, are absolutely incredible,” Oxenham said.
He said the narrowing capability gap makes private enterprise AI viable while allowing enterprises to maintain cost control and keep their AI workloads under their control.
For SUSE, the choice of AI models and services is therefore part of the same sovereignty question as the choice of silicon—enterprises need the ability to change what they depend on.
India moves AI from experimentation toward production
In India, SUSE sees the sovereignty discussion alongside a growing need to move AI workloads from experimentation into production. SUSE identifies two customer categories for its AI Factory platform in India—service providers and end users.
Service providers have traditionally provided infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) and are now offering GPU as a service. “These service providers really need a platform,” Marshal Correia, general manager for India and South Asia, said. “The IndiaAI Mission’s compute initiative has helped make enough GPUs available to data center providers in India.”
The second category is end users. These customers have experimented with use cases and now need a platform as those use cases scale. Cloud-native technology plays a major role in this layer.
“Underneath LLM and above the hardware, that is the layer that we are working on,” Correia said. “This has, of course, a lot of tools, slicing, dicing, etc., security.”
A large amount of work last year focused on proofs of concept, with some moving into production and many not making that transition. With greater availability of GPUs and infrastructure, SUSE sees an opportunity for customers to establish a platform or software factory that can support a growing number of applications.
SUSE also sees demand from enterprises building their own infrastructure for generative AI, MLOps, and domain-specific workloads such as computer vision, as well as from organizations building multi-tenant infrastructure such as gigafactories, neoclouds, and public-sector systems.
Oxenham added that these customers need infrastructure for workload isolation, access control, observability, and security. Enterprises running their own AI workloads also need a platform on which applications can move from experimentation into production, he said.
Sovereignty differs by region
SUSE’s definition of sovereignty also varies by market, although Oxenham said the underlying need for control is common across regions.
In the U.S., private, customer-controlled infrastructure is largely driven by commercial velocity, IP protection, and financial predictability. CIOs want to eliminate unpredictable consumption-based API costs, avoid vendor lock-in, and maintain deployment flexibility.
In Europe, the driver is heavily precautionary and regulatory. It is anchored in compliance, data sovereignty, and risk-tiering under the EU AI Act, along with a desire to diversify from incumbent hardware and software ecosystems.
In India, the drivers include national AI ambitions and regulatory requirements, while customers also face the practical challenge of moving AI applications from experimentation into production.
Oxenham said he sees sovereignty less as a binary switch based purely on data residency or jurisdiction, and more as a spectrum rooted in operational resilience, pivotability, and active risk management.
“Viewing sovereignty solely through the lens of data location misses the bigger picture,” he said. “True sovereignty is about evaluating tradeoffs at every layer of the stack so an organization is never locked in or left at the mercy of external constraints.”
That includes third-party Linux, orchestration, AI frameworks, models, and silicon.
Air-gapped deployments add another layer of control
The question of dependency becomes more direct in air-gapped environments, where enterprises need to keep data, model artifacts, and system activity within an isolated network.
SUSE said its AI Factory architecture supports such deployments, with SUSE Security and SUSE Observability used to enforce and monitor network and system boundaries. Software updates can be staged through signed artifact bundles in local registries.
“For fully disconnected deployments, this pre-validated architecture makes updates mechanically straightforward,” Oxenham said. “Because the entire stack is tested and verified as a single unit, customers simply mirror or stage the signed artifact bundles into local registries within their isolated network.”
Air-gapped deployments illustrate the same distinction. The external technology does not disappear. Instead, the enterprise controls what enters the environment and how the software is operated and updated once inside it.
The central tradeoff remains—an enterprise can retain control over its data, infrastructure, and higher-level software layers while still depending on Nvidia, AMD, or another accelerator vendor for silicon-specific components.
For SUSE, sovereignty therefore rests less on eliminating dependency and more on preserving the ability to change dependencies when needed.

articles.title: « 4,1 fois moins de chances d'avoir un accident » Tesla publie ses données de sécurité pour le FSD
articles.text:
Sur son compte X dédié au marché européen, Tesla a publié ce 1er septembre 2026 un bilan chiffré du FSD (Full Self-Driving) « Supervised ». Selon la firme d’Elon Musk, il s’agit du dossier exact qui a été présenté à tous les États membres en avril 2026, après l’autorisation du logiciel aux Pays-Bas.
Ces chiffres tombent quelques semaines avant un rendez-vous que Tesla ne veut pas manquer. En effet, l’Union européenne doit trancher sur l’autorisation du FSD dans les 27 pays de l’Union européenne lors d’un vote attendu début octobre. Le constructeur cherche à convaincre les États encore réticents. Pour être adopté, le texte doit réunir au moins 15 des 27 pays représentant 65 % de la population européenne.
Près d’1,3 million de km parcourus en FSD avant son autorisation
Dans le détail, Tesla souligne que le FSD a parcouru 1 276 209 km « avec zéro collision » lors des tests routiers sous la supervision de ses ingénieurs. Parmi les autres indicateurs d’une conduite plus sûre, le constructeur américain souligne :
- La réduction de 77 % à 97 % de l’intervention du freinage automatique d’urgence (AEB)
- Moins d’accélérations et de freinages intempestifs
- Moins d’utilisation du klaxon
- Plus d’utilisation des clignotants
À l’heure actuelle, la marque annonce que le FSD est utilisé par plus de 70 000 propriétaires de Tesla répartis dans les cinq pays où il est autorisé. Avec plus d’1 million de km parcourus quotidiennement, le logiciel aurait « 4,1 fois moins de chances d’avoir un accident comparé à un conducteur humain ».
Par ailleurs, Tesla précise dans son rapport que sur 708 échantillons européens où le système a dépassé la limite détectée, la voiture en FSD roulait « à ou en dessous de la vitesse médiane du trafic environnant dans 98 % des cas à haute vitesse et n’a jamais dépassé le véhicule le plus rapide dans 99,9 % des cas ». Ce point du dépassement des limitations de vitesse est l’un des freins majeurs à l’adoption du logiciel pour de nombreux pays, dont la France.
Des limites sur les chiffres de Tesla
Les inquiétudes autour de l’homologation du FSD tiennent également à l’origine de ces données. Ces dernières viennent de Tesla, et d’elle seule. Aucun régulateur indépendant ne les a validées publiquement. Si la marque veut jouer la carte de la transparence avant le vote en publiant ses données de sécurité, il lui manque toujours une validation indépendante.
En l’occurrence, le rapport n’inclut pas les données de conduite de la flotte des 70 000 véhicules particuliers européens, alors que le constructeur partage bien des chiffres pour l’Amérique du Nord. Pourtant, ce n’est pas la première fois que Tesla dégaine ses statistiques maison. Fin juillet 2026, le constructeur communiquait déjà un FSD avec « 3,5 fois moins de collisions » que la conduite manuelle aux Pays-Bas. Des données basées, donc, sur la conduite des propriétaires.
Une Europe divisée, un enjeu commercial
Le vote est loin d’être gagné. La France a fermé la porte au FSD tant qu’il n’aura pas d’homologation européenne, une position rejointe par l’Espagne. À l’inverse, la Finlande envisageait de donner son feu vert au niveau national. Les États européens n’ont clairement pas la même lecture d’un même logiciel, et il suffit d’une poignée de refus pour faire capoter la double majorité exigée.
La défiance ne vient pas seulement des États. Le Conseil européen pour la sécurité des transports (ETSC) a écrit dès le 12 juin 2026 aux ministres des Transports de l’UE pour leur demander de ne pas reconnaître l’homologation néerlandaise tant que des preuves de sécurité concrètes n’auront pas été rendues publiques. La Suède, de son côté, a laissé entendre qu’elle pourrait s’y opposer à cause de la gestion des limitations de vitesse par le logiciel.
Pour Tesla, l’enjeu dépasse la seule question technique. Le constructeur cherche à reconquérir des parts de marché sur un continent où ses ventes ont reculé face à la concurrence chinoise, même si certains l’enterrent un peu vite. Le FSD est un argument commercial de poids, et publier des chiffres flatteurs avant le vote fait partie de la manœuvre. Sans données indépendantes pour les confronter, les régulateurs qui diront oui le feront en partie sur parole.

articles.title: Cette mise à jour d'Android Auto pose de sérieuses questions de sécurité routière
articles.text:
S'il est interdit d'utiliser son téléphone au volant, de nombreux véhicules modernes sont dotés d'un écran central tactile de la taille d'un iPad. Avec Android Auto et CarPlay, connecter son téléphone est facile, rapide, et permet de répondre "en toute sécurité" à ses contacts. Mais à proposer trop de fonctionnalités, certaines ne deviendraient-elles pas dangereuses ?
Le remplacement de Google Assistant par Gemini dans Android Auto, opéré par Google il y a quelques mois, divise les utilisateurs. Plusieurs conducteurs estiment que ce changement augmente les risques de distraction au volant.
Gemini manquerait de fiabilité ?
Selon des retours d’utilisateurs, notamment sur le forum Reddit r/GoogleAssistant, Gemini serait moins fiable que son prédécesseur pour exécuter des commandes simples. Certains doivent répéter ou reformuler leurs demandes, ce qui prolonge l’interaction et détourne leur attention de la route.
Un utilisateur, L00k_Again, va jusqu’à suggérer que cette situation pourrait favoriser les accidents ou les comportements agressifs au volant. Depuis son déploiement en avril, les plaintes concernant les performances de Gemini se multiplient, sans amélioration notable de la part de Google, selon les utilisateurs.
L'utilisateur plus concentré sur l'appli que sur la route ?
Google a tenté de corriger certains dysfonctionnements, mais les problèmes persistent. L’argument avancé est que chaque échec de compréhension ou d’exécution de la part de Gemini oblige le conducteur à s’investir davantage dans la conversation, ce qui pourrait, à terme, accroître le risque de distraction.
Contrairement à Google Assistant, conçu pour des commandes courtes et limitées, Gemini est capable de gérer des requêtes plus longues et complexes. Cette approche plus conversationnelle pourrait inciter les conducteurs à interagir plus longtemps avec l’assistant, augmentant ainsi les risques de dysfonctionnement.
"C'est normal, Gemini est naturel" selon Google
Google défend pour sa part le caractère naturel de Gemini, qui, selon l’entreprise, devrait réduire la distraction. Cependant, certains utilisateurs soulignent que l’assistant peine parfois à accomplir des tâches que Google Assistant maîtrisait sans difficulté.
Si aucune preuve tangible ne démontre que Gemini augmente objectivement le risque d’accidents par rapport à Google Assistant, son fonctionnement plus interactif pourrait, selon certains, alourdir la charge mentale du conducteur et à terme, diminuer sa concentration sur la conduite.

Der größte Umbruch des Jahres liegt im Verhalten der Nutzer:innen selbst. Viele von ihnen googeln nicht mehr, sondern lassen sich ihre Antworten direkt von KI-Systemen geben. Für Agenturen bedeutet das ein Umdenken, denn Inhalte müssen heute so aufbereitet sein, dass Antwortmaschinen sie als Quelle erkennen und zitieren. Parallel dazu übernehmen KI-Agenten immer mehr Aufgaben, die bisher Menschen am Bildschirm erledigt haben. Sie buchen Termine, vergleichen Angebote und wickeln Serviceanfragen vollständig ab, weshalb eine gute Website inzwischen für Menschen und Maschinen gleichermaßen funktionieren muss.
Zugleich hat die massenhafte Verfügbarkeit von KI-Werkzeugen einen Gegentrend ausgelöst. Wenn sich Websites in wenigen Minuten erstellen lassen, sehen viele am Ende fast gleich aus. Erfolgreiche Agenturen setzen deshalb auf unverwechselbare Gestaltung und eine klare Markenhaltung, während generative Interfaces im Hintergrund Inhalte und Layouts in Echtzeit auf die jeweiligen Besucher:innen zuschneiden.
So entsteht die Bewertung
Hinter der Auszeichnung steht ein Punktesystem, das jede Bewerbung anhand von 531 Kriterien aus den Bereichen Design, Know-how und Kundenzufriedenheit misst. Am Ende erhält jede Agentur einen Wert zwischen 1 und 10, wobei die Auszeichnung ab einer Punktzahl von 6,90 vergeben wird.
Was die besten Agenturen auszeichnet
Die ausgezeichneten Agenturen zeigen, dass sich Technologie und eigene Handschrift nicht ausschließen. Sie nutzen KI dort, wo sie Arbeit beschleunigt und Ergebnisse verbessert, und setzen zugleich auf eigenständige Konzepte, die Marken langfristig tragen.

Unter dem Anspruch ‚Building brands people love‘ verbindet pechschwarz® Branding, Webdesign und digitales Marketing zu einer differenzierenden, kohärenten Digital Brand Experience. articles.title: Jagdish Farshan raises Rs 43.5 cr led by Sharrp Ventures
articles.text:
Jagdish Farshan raises Rs 43.5 Cr led by Sharrp Ventures
This Gujarat based regional snack brand will use this capital for expansion related activities
Jagdish Farshan, the Gujarat based snack brand has raised Rs 43.5 crore in a Series A round of funding led by Sharrp Ventures, the investment office of Harsh Mariwala, Founder and Chairman of Marico Limited, alongside a group of angel investors.
Jagdish Farshan will deploy this capital towards geographic expansion, manufacturing and supply-chain capacity, retail and institutional distribution, technology and digital commerce.
This is the first institutional capital raised by Jagdish Farshan as the company looks to expand beyond the state of Gujarat. It currently operates 27 retail outlets across central Gujarat, alongside two outlets in North America.
On the funding raised, Jagdish Farshan CEO Aakash Kandoi said, “This fundraise is about building Jagdish Farshan for the next 100 years. We have a strong foundation of consumer trust, product quality and a deep understanding of the Indian snacks and sweets category. We are now at a point where we can take what we have built in Gujarat and scale it across the country, without compromising on the qualities that have made the brand relevant for generations.”
Established in 1938, the range of products by Jagdish Farshan include snacks, namkeen and sweets. It has a portfolio of 500+ products/SKUs and a presence across multiple markets, supported by manufacturing capabilities and an expanding distribution network across retail and institutional channels.
The statement said the investment has come at a time when established regional food brands are seeking to move beyond regional markets by investing in organised manufacturing, wider distribution and digital-first channels. In this market, Jagdish Farshan aims to combine its product heritage and regional strength with a modern operating platform to deepen existing markets and expand into new geographies.
Divya Gupta, Principal, Sharrp Ventures, said: “Jagdish Farshan combines decades of consumer trust and product heritage with the opportunity to build a much larger organised food business.”

articles.title: Cronos blockchain restarts after $74 million Tectonic exploit
articles.text:
The Cronos blockchain network has resumed trading activity after a price-manipulation attack on the Tectonic cryptocurrency lending platform allowed an attacker to borrow $74 million.
According to current information, the threat actor artificially inflated the price of Tectonic’s TONIC token by 100 times, then used it as collateral to borrow real assets. The price manipulation happened in 20 minutes.
Despite the massive amount the exploit generated, the attacker only managed to steal roughly $6 million worth of Ethereum, the rest of the funds being “stuck” on Cronos, says blockchain security and data analytics company PeckShield.
Cronos is an Ethereum-like blockchain network associated with Crypto.com, while Tectonic is a decentralized finance (DeFi) lending app running on Cronos.
Tectonic, which was Cronos’ largest lending protocol before the incident, holding $122 million, allows users to deposit cryptocurrency and borrow against assets they provide as collateral.
After the incident, the total value locked according to DeFiLlama is just under $3 million.
Yesterday, Tectonic announced that it was investigating an incident and advised users not to interact with the protocol until the platform publicly confirmed that it was safe to do so.
Cronos responded quickly to the detected exploit and halted the blockchain’s operation, freezing all transactions in progress at the time.
Earlier today, Cronos restarted the network again and notified users that it “is producing blocks again and is fully back online.”
“This was a validator-consensus emergency action to protect users from an exploit on the Tectonic protocol,” Cronos states.
“The chain state was restored to before the Tectonic exploit from this morning. Cronos is producing blocks again as of 2026-08-30 23:49:01 UTC, starting from block 90,896,189.”
The blockchain is currently being closely monitored for stability, protocol compatibility, and other issues.
The platform also said it would provide further details about the exploit in a post-mortem report to be published soon.

articles.title: Vehículos autónomos Zoox están lesionando a los conductores que prueban los autos antes de salir al mercado
articles.text:
La proliferación de vehículos autónomos en las calles de ciudades como Los Ángeles o San Francisco está transformando la movilidad urbana, pero el avance tecnológico convive con una realidad menos visible: los conductores de prueba aún son esenciales para operar estos automóviles y su seguridad laboral está siendo cuestionada.
Un reporte reciente indica que los empleados que supervisan y prueban modelos de Waymo y Zoox han sufrido lesiones, lo que plantea interrogantes sobre el impacto de la automatización en el bienestar humano.
PUBLICIDAD
Lesiones laborales en la industria de vehículos autónomos: datos y causas
Un informe publicado por TechCrunch, que cita datos de la Administración de Seguridad y Salud Ocupacional (OSHA), revela que Waymo y Zoox, compañía perteneciente a Amazon, notificaron más de 20 incidentes en los que empleados resultaron lesionados durante pruebas en sus vehículos autónomos.
La mayoría de las lesiones estuvieron relacionadas con maniobras inesperadas, como frenazos o cambios bruscos de dirección, situaciones comunes cuando se prueba software que aún no está completamente pulido para la conducción sin intervención humana.
PUBLICIDAD
Entre los daños sufridos por los conductores de prueba se incluyen esguinces, dolores de espalda y latigazos cervicales. Estos incidentes han ido en aumento conforme las empresas expanden sus operaciones a nuevas ciudades y suman más kilómetros de pruebas.
Los conductores de prueba son operadores humanos contratados por las empresas de tecnología que viajan a bordo de los vehículos de desarrollo para supervisar su funcionamiento en el mundo real.
PUBLICIDAD
Especialmente, se observa una mayor incidencia en mercados prioritarios para el sector, como Phoenix, Los Ángeles y San Francisco, donde la circulación de estos vehículos de prueba es cada vez más frecuente.
La diversidad de vehículos utilizados para las pruebas también es un factor relevante. No siempre se emplean modelos específicamente diseñados para la conducción autónoma, como el Waymo Jaguar I-Pace, el Zoox Robotaxi o el nuevo Ojai.
PUBLICIDAD
En muchos casos, los ensayos se realizan en automóviles modificados, como el Toyota Highlander adaptado con sensores y sistemas de software experimental, lo que puede incrementar la probabilidad de movimientos imprevistos y, en consecuencia, de accidentes laborales.
Impacto de la expansión acelerada de vehículos autónomos en las ciudades
La rápida extensión de los ensayos con vehículos autónomos pone en evidencia que, tanto las ciudades como las empresas, enfrentan desafíos logísticos y de seguridad. Los incidentes reportados muestran que la infraestructura urbana y los protocolos internos de las tecnológicas no siempre están preparados para el ritmo de crecimiento de la industria.
PUBLICIDAD
Esto se traduce en una dificultad para garantizar la seguridad de los conductores de prueba y, eventualmente, de los pasajeros de estos futuros servicios.
Los organismos federales de seguridad han comenzado a investigar los incidentes relacionados con vehículos autónomos que ya circulan sin conductor.
Este escenario podría obligar a las empresas a reducir el ritmo de despliegue de nuevas unidades y a revisar sus estrategias de expansión, priorizando el desarrollo de software y la capacitación en seguridad para los empleados que aún intervienen en el proceso.
PUBLICIDAD
Perspectivas para la industria automotriz y el rol de la regulación
La relevancia de la conducción autónoma no se limita a grandes empresas como Waymo, Zoox, Uber o Tesla. Fabricantes más pequeños de vehículos eléctricos como Lucid y Rivian, así como grandes conglomerados como Hyundai, consideran que el sector autónomo será clave para su crecimiento en los próximos años.
En este contexto, se prevé que instituciones como la OSHA incrementen la vigilancia sobre las condiciones laborales de los conductores de prueba, exigiendo mayores estándares de seguridad y protocolos de prevención.
PUBLICIDAD
La evolución de la industria dependerá en gran medida de la capacidad de las empresas para equilibrar la innovación tecnológica con la protección de los trabajadores que actualmente hacen posible el desarrollo de los vehículos autónomos.

articles.title: La Dacia Sandero va passer à l’électrique, mais pas que : voici ce que l’on sait déjà — Frandroid
articles.text:
Lorsqu’il s’agit de la voiture électrique, les constructeurs automobiles se divisent en deux catégories. D’un côté, nous retrouvons les marques qui proposent les mêmes modèles, déclinés en plusieurs motorisations. C’est par exemple le cas de Peugeot.
De l’autre, nous avons des entreprises qui font le choix de créer des gammes spécifiques. On pense par exemple à Volkswagen ou Renault. C’est aussi le cas de Dacia, qui fait partie de cette deuxième catégorie. Pour mémoire, la firme commercialise actuellement sa Spring, qui devrait bientôt être épaulée par la nouvelle Hipster.
Mais la marque low-cost devrait désormais changer son fusil d’épaule, comme l’indique le site AutoExpress. Ce dernier relaie les propos de Lina Ribeiro, directrice générale de la filiale britannique de Dacia.
Votre production solaire dépasse votre consommation ? Le SolarFlow 2400 AC+ stocke automatiquement votre surplus dans vos batteries. 100 % compatible avec la grande majorité des installations solaires en toiture, il permet de faire évoluer votre système simplement et à moindre coût.
Cette dernière confirme que la prochaine génération de la citadine, prévue pour 2028, aura bien droit à plusieurs motorisations. Même son de cloche du côté de Katrin Adt, directrice générale de Dacia. Celle-ci indique que si rien n’a encore été finalisé, Dacia travaille à des solutions permettant d’adopter « une seule plateforme pour tous les [modèles] ».
L’idée n’est pas neuve. Il y a environ un an et demi, l’ancien patron de Dacia, Denis Le Vot, évoquait déjà une Sandero disponible à la fois en thermique et en électrique, jugeant que le marché n’était pas encore prêt à basculer entièrement vers l’électrique et que les versions à combustion seraient « très probablement toutes hybrides ». Ses successeurs ne font donc que confirmer une trajectoire déjà tracée.
Ainsi, la future Sandero devrait reprendre la base CMF-B déjà bien connue, mais qui pourrait avoir droit à des modifications. Le best-seller de la marque reprendrait des motorisations essence et hybrides déjà présentes sur les Renault Clio et autres Dacia Duster. Mais surtout, elle se déclinerait pour la toute première fois en électrique. Dans cette configuration, il se murmure qu’elle hériterait de certaines technologies des R5 E-Tech et Twingo. Mais dans quelle mesure ?
Cette Sandero électrique ne débarque pas seule : Dacia a confirmé vouloir lancer quatre voitures 100 % électriques d’ici 2030, chacune dérivée d’un modèle déjà au catalogue plutôt que d’une gamme inédite. La nouvelle Spring ouvre le bal l’an prochain, la Sandero suivra en 2028, et un Duster électrique devrait fermer la marche en fin de décennie. Katrin Adt vise d’ailleurs deux tiers de volumes électrifiés pour la marque à l’horizon 2030.
Encore un peu de patience
Le média britannique explique que la future Dacia Sandero électrique devrait reprendre les plus petites batteries, afin de conserver un prix abordable. Pour mémoire, celle de la R5 E-Tech affiche une capacité de 40 kWh et offre une autonomie maximale de 315 kilomètres selon le cycle WLTP. De son côté, la Twingo embarque une batterie LFP (lithium-fer-phosphate) de 27,5 kWh. De quoi parcourir jusqu’à 262 kilomètres en une seule charge.
Dans les deux cas, la recharge s’effectue en une trentaine de minutes environ. Mais pour le moment, Dacia n’a encore rien acté. Sa patronne rappelle d’ailleurs que la future Sandero est « encore en phase de développement ». Nous devrions avoir plus de nouvelles au cours de l’année 2028. Une chose est sûre, l’accent devrait être mis sur le rapport qualité / prix, puisque la firme est réputée pour son positionnement très abordable. Le but sera de « trouver l’équilibre entre performance et accessibilité ».
L’objectif, comme l’indique Dacia, est de « démocratiser l’accès aux véhicules électriques ». Il se dit également que le style sera identique quelle que soit la motorisation, même si les versions zéro émission (à l’échappement) devraient se distinguer par une calandre pleine et des poignées affleurantes. Cela dans le but d’optimiser le Cx (coefficient de traînée). Une version Stepway surélevée serait également au programme pour cette prochaine génération de la citadine.

Let’s dive in.
Become smarter about tech and commerce in Francophone Africa, and the policies shaping them. Read previous editions here first and subscribe below.
M&A
South Africa’s Nedbank gets CBK’s approval to acquire 66% of Kenyan lender NCBA
Remember the proposed acquisition of Kenyan digital-first bank NCBA by South African tier-1 lender Nedbank that has hogged headlines since the start of the year?
We’ve got a big development in that saga. On Monday, the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) said it had approved Nedbank’s acquisition of up to 66% of NCBA on August 28, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for the South African lender. The approval follows months of regulatory reviews and a shareholder offer that saw NCBA investors accept Nedbank’s proposal in exchange for cash and Nedbank shares.
State of play: The deal isn’t fully closed yet, but once completed, Nedbank will take control of NCBA, giving the South African lender a major foothold in East Africa. Nedbank will become NCBA’s majority owner, while the remaining 34% will stay in public hands. The Kenyan digital-first bank will also retain its brand, local management, and Nairobi headquarters.
Explain like I’m new here: In January, Nedbank announced that it wanted to acquire about two-thirds of NCBA through a tender offer, asking existing NCBA shareholders to offer up their shares for sale. Under the proposed deal, shareholders would receive 20% cash and 80% newly issued Nedbank shares. The offer opened in May and closed on July 10, with NCBA shareholders offering 1.32 billion shares, equivalent to 79.9% of NCBA.
However, shareholders offered more shares than Nedbank’s 66% target, so the bank had to scale back the allocation to 1.09 billion shares, leaving some shareholders unable to sell their shares to Nedbank.
Why does Nedbank want NCBA? NCBA gives Nedbank an established presence across East Africa. It has banking subsidiaries in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda, plus a joint venture in Côte d’Ivoire. NCBA reported KES 12.4 billion ($95.7 million) in profit after tax in H1 2026, while its total assets reached KES 739 billion ($5.7 billion).
Nedbank also sees the acquisition as a way to get closer to other East African and nearby markets it is eyeing, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ethiopia.
Is this the end of the road? Not yet. CBK’s approval clears a major hurdle, but the deal still has a few other regulatory, banking, and market conduct conditions to meet before it can be completed. Nedbank previously said it expects the deal to finalise by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Fintech
Nigerian fintech Allawee folds into Paystack after 2025 acquisition
Customers of Nigerian card-issuing fintech Allawee have until November 30 to move their money, replace their cards, and tell anyone who pays them that their account details are changing, the startup wrote in an email. Allawee has since been folded into Paystack’s operations.
What happened? Paystack, the Stripe-backed payments company, acquired Allawee in a 2025 deal that was not publicly announced. Allawee will close its personal and business account services on December 1, 2026; its cards will stop working, and payments sent to its virtual account numbers issued on its platform will fail. Customers will need to withdraw their balances, update their bank details with senders, and replace saved card details on subscriptions before the deadline.
Businesses are being directed to Paystack MFB, its parent company’s microfinance bank, while individuals are being directed to Zap, Paystack’s consumer transfer app. Balances, account numbers, transaction history, and verification records will not move across automatically, so customers opening new accounts will start again.
Explain like I’m new here: Allawee launched in 2022 as a credit-card lender; it later pivoted to credit-risk software before settling on card infrastructure, enabling other fintechs to issue and manage cards.
By May 2025, it was providing services to Nigerian fintechs such as PiggyVest, Nomba, and Carbon, letting them launch cards in weeks instead of months. That infrastructure is likely more valuable to Paystack than Allawee’s consumer accounts. Once Paystack had its own microfinance bank, Allawee’s Providus Bank-backed accounts were competing with products Paystack could offer itself. Acquiring Allawee lets Paystack take the useful infrastructure while moving customers onto the banking products it now controls.
Zoom out: Allawee is the second fintech brand Paystack has folded into its operations this year, after absorbing Nigerian business-banking startup Brass in June. Nigeria’s fintech market seems to be moving from “build everything” to “buy the missing pieces.” For customers, that can mean better-connected products, but also the inconvenience of being moved between companies, setups, and platforms whenever these changes happen.

Fintech
Yele Bademosi transitions to Chairman at Nigerian fintech Onboard Global
Yele Bademosi is transitioning from chief executive officer to the chairman’s seat at Onboard Global, the Nigerian stablecoin-based fintech startup that launched in 2022.
Onboard lets users spend stablecoins like everyday money, using cards and stablecoin-to-fiat payment accounts. The fintech spun out of Nestcoin, a Web3 banking platform Bademosi co-founded in 2021.
Between the lines: On Monday, Bademosi announced that he was stepping down as Onboard’s chief executive officer and taking up a new role as chairman. Paul Oladimeji, who has worked on Onboard’s products and infrastructure, will take over the day-to-day running of the company. The leadership transition and Oladimeji’s background point to a handover from founder-led direction to product-led execution.
State of play: Bademosi co-founded Onboard when stablecoins and cryptocurrency wallets were still the centre of the company’s pitch. The business is now trying to build something broader: financial infrastructure that connects local currencies, dollars, and stablecoins for individuals and businesses.
Zoom out: Onboard is entering a more demanding phase of its growth. Moving from a consumer wallet into payments, business accounts, and financial infrastructure means competing for customers while navigating the licencing and compliance requirements that come with moving real money across borders. Bademosi’s move gives the company a chance to put a new operator at the helm as it makes that transition.

Digital Infrastructure
Namibia launches DigiNam to let citizens prove their identity and sign documents online
Having to enter your name, submit an ID, and fill out the same forms every time you access a government service is a real pain. It gets worse when you make the trip to an office only to realise you left one crucial document at home.
It’s one of the reasons blockchain bros have been clamouring for decentralised identity (DID), which allows you to prove who you are once and use that identity across different services without carrying files or memorising your ID number.
Well, it’s not quite DID, but Namibia wants to make some of that hassle disappear.
What happened? On Monday, Namibia launched DigiNam, a national digital trust system that will let people prove their identity and sign online. The system is built around the country’s National Public Key Infrastructure (NPKI), the technology and rules that help verify digital identities and electronic signatures. Namibia’s Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety, and Security; the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology (ICT); and the Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia (CRAN), the country’s telecoms regulator, are behind the rollout.
Explain like I’m new here: Think of DigiNam as a verified identity for the Internet. Once electronic IDs are issued through the system, they can carry digital credentials that let a government agency verify that you are really you when you use an online service. The system can confirm that an electronic signature belongs to the person who signed a document and that the document has not been changed afterwards.
Why did Namibia bother? Today, accessing many services can mean proving who you are over and over again. Namibia wants authorised government agencies to securely cross-check information, so citizens do not have to keep submitting the same documents or visiting offices in person.
However, moving more services online also creates a trust problem. In H1 2025, 65% of Namibians reported being targeted online, by email, phone call, or text messaging fraud, according to TransUnion Africa, a risk management agency. Between April and June 2026, the country also recorded over 500,000 cyber vulnerabilities.
What happens next? CRAN will oversee the trust system as the “Root Certification Authority,” setting standards and approving organisations that can issue trusted digital credentials. The Ministry of Home Affairs will be the first to roll out those credentials. Namibia plans to eventually connect more government services and extend the system to sectors such as financial services and telecoms.

articles.title: "Chulos, prepotentes y sabelotodos": si la pregunta es si existe 'madrileñofobia' en España ya tenemos la respuesta
articles.text:
Contra todo pronóstico y probablemente para pasmo de sus propietarios, en 2024 el Puerto Martina, un pequeño restaurante de Mera (Galicia), se convirtió en noticia de alcance internacional. Hablaban de él en la prensa, en los telediarios e incluso The Guardian le dedicó un extenso artículo. El motivo no era su comida o lo bien que tiraba las cañas. No. Si el negocio se volvió viral es porque anunció a bombo y platillo su decisión de cerrar en agosto para evitar así a los turistas del centro del país. "Si cae una bomba en Mera se quedan sin tontos en la Meseta", ironizaba en el post de Facebook en el que avanza la clausura del local.
Los dueños del bar lamentaban la "prepotencia" de ciertos turistas y aseguraban estar "hartos de los madrileños". Aquel episodio dejó botando una pregunta que no es ni mucho menos nueva... ¿Puede hablarse de madrileñofobia en España?
Un porcentaje: 68,5%. El año pasado Zity, una compañía de carsharing, se propuso un desafío curioso: estudiar la madrileñofobia. O mejor dicho, averiguar si existe como tal y cuál es su alcance. Con ese propósito, entrevistó a algo más de 1.100 personas, echó mano de algunos datos del INE y elaboró luego un informe de 31 páginas no exento de humor en el que desgrana algunas claves.
¿La más interesante? Que el 68,5% de los madrileños creen que se les trata de forma distinta cuando se van de vacaciones a otras regiones del país.
"Como una plaga". No es la única conclusión del estudio. Por ejemplo, los autores del informe comprobaron que el 59,5% de los habitantes de la capital reconocen sentirse incómodos cuando se habla del "'turismo madrileño' como si fuera una plaga" y que algunos incluso optan por ocultar su origen cuando salen de casa. No son mayoría, pero un tercio de los madrileños admite que es una práctica que hacen siempre, alguna vez o se les ha pasado por la cabeza.
Lo más curioso es que la mayoría de los turistas que parten de Madrid se consideran visitantes educados y correctos. Así se ve de hecho cerca del 53%.
Cuando Zity fue más allá y preguntó a los madrileños si alguna vez se habían sentido desplazados se llevó otra sorpresa: del 50,5% respondió que sí. En teoría, el 43% percibió ese trato diferente solo en algunas comunidades, pero el restante 7,5% aseguró que es una sensación habitual. Por supuesto ese dato tiene otra cara más amable: el 49,5% de los madrileños nunca se ha sentido marginado.
¿Y cómo los ve el resto? El estudio de Zity (compañía que por cierto se ha despedido de Madrid este año) es únicamente eso, un estudio, con sus sesgos y limitaciones evidentes; pero resulta interesante porque aporta un doble enfoque: nos muestra cómo se sienten los madrileños cuando viajan a Galicia, Alicante, Baleares, Canarias… Y cómo los ve en esos lugares la población local.
Según el estudio, más de un tercio de los encuestados (el 35,5%) cree que los madrileños son los turistas que peor actitud tienen cuando veranean en otras regiones, lo que convierte a la capital en "el lugar de procedencia de los turistas con peor comportamiento". El dato supera con creces al 21,3% que considera que los turistas más maleducados son los catalanes o el 13,3% de los andaluces.
Bajando al detalle. Si nos fijamos en las respuestas por comunidades hay más sorpresas. Si hablamos solo con gallegos el 53,6% señalan a los madrileños como los visitantes con peor actitud del país. Con todo, el estudio vuelve a tener una 'cara B' reveladora: aunque muchos señalan a los madrileños o catalanes como los peores veraneantes, uno de cada cuatro encuestados cree que los turistas que peor se portan durante las vacaciones son las personas de su propia región.
Sí, hay madrileñofobia. Otra de las revelaciones del informe es que, efectivamente, la madrileñofobia parece ser un fenómeno real que no se limita a la percepción de los madrileños. Así lo considera casi la mitad de los encuestados (46,7%), sobre todo los residentes de Galicia, la Comunidad Valenciana y la propia Madrid, que aseguran que se trata de un problema innegable.
Es más, el 45,8% asegura haber presenciado alguna situación negativa hacia los turistas madrileños y más de la mitad (el 51,1%) han visto en redes comentarios críticos o de tono satírico sobre cómo actúan los madrileños en verano. Son datos contundentes que chocan con otro igual de llamativo: el 80% de la población que vive fuera de Madrid cree que no trata diferente a los turistas de la capital.
"Chulo, prepotente y sabelotodo". Los hosteleros de Mera que se hicieron virales en 2024 por su "hartazgo" lamentaban la "prepotencia" y "altivez" de los turistas. No son los únicos que parecen opinar así. Cuando Zity preguntó a sus encuestados qué tres adjetivos describen mejor al turista madrileño se encontró con una lista muy poco edificante. Los calificativos más comunes fueron "chulo" (37,5%), "prepotente" (36,5%) y "sabelotodo" (29,2%). Si ampliamos la lista hay otros algo más positivos, como "cosmopolita" (22,5%) o "sociable" (20,9%).
Muchos encuestados también habían escuchado frases como "Esto en Madrid no pasa" (68,5%), "No hay mejor agua que la de Madrid" (64,2%) o comentarios sobre "la arrogancia" de los madrileños y que todo les parece "pequeño o cutre".
Si hay una coletilla que los encuestados admiten haber escuchado a menudo es "Ya están aquí los de Madrid" (70,7%), lo que da una idea de la imagen que tienen en otras regiones del país. Si hablamos de Galicia el tópico más extendido es que los madrileños "aparcan en cualquier sitio", lo que conecta con casos de coches aparcados en zonas costeras que acaban anegados cuando sube la marea.
💢 La madrileñofobia en verano: «Vámonos al Prado con banderas gallegas a cantar babosadas»
«El modelo turístico de Madrid es nuestra ruina y la peregrinación nacionalcatolicista resulta sencillamente inasumible» https://t.co/hNOKD4Qltu
Un runrún de fondo. Aunque el debate torno a la madrileñofobia sonó con fuerza en 2025 a raíz del estudio de Zity, la realidad es que no es nuevo. Todo lo contrario. El tema resurge de forma periódica, a menudo a calor de la actualidad. En 2021, por ejemplo, con las restricciones a la movilidad por el COVID-19 como telón de fondo, la presidenta de la región, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, denunció que la comunidad estaba sufriendo "una madrileñofobia nunca vista".
La polémica volvió a emerger años después por el cartel del bar de Mera y lo sigue haciendo cada cierto tiempo, casi siempre en verano, coincidiendo con la temporada alta del turismo. Hace poco El Debate hablaba del tema a raíz de un tuit en el que se cuestionaba la saturación de Santiago y El Español hacía algo similar usando como gancho un vídeo irónico sobre el turismo en Galicia.
Una versión anterior de este artículo se publicó en agosto de 2025.

articles.title: 9.5 Million Impacted by Aesto Health Data Breach
articles.text:
More than 9.5 million people had their personal and health information stolen in a data breach at healthcare technology company Aesto Health.
Based in Birmingham, Alabama, Aesto Health offers secure data migration, electronic health record (EHR) exchanges, and legacy data archiving services to healthcare providers and medical practices.
The data breach, the company said in a June 2026 incident notice, was discovered on December 18, 2025, and involved portions of its Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure.
“Upon detecting the unauthorized activity, we immediately contained the incident and commenced a thorough investigation. As part of our investigation, we engaged leading cybersecurity experts to identify what personal information, if any, was involved,” Aesto Health said.
On May 26, 2026, the company’s investigation determined that hackers exfiltrated personally identifiable information (PII) and protected health information (PHI) between December 2 and 18.
The compromised information includes names, Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, other ID numbers, dates of birth, financial account numbers, medical information, health insurance information, and taxpayer identification numbers.
Aesto Health has notified the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) that 9,540,683 individuals are impacted by the data breach. HHS added the company to its data breach portal on Monday.
At least two dozen Aesto Health healthcare provider clients across several states have been affected by the incident, some of which have chosen to notify the potentially affected people themselves.
